I would like to understand the differences between traditional and self-publishing. How do I know which route to go? Which route has the potential for a greater profit?

1	Your two main options are traditional publishing with a publishing company, or self-publishing
     2	through a platform like IngramSpark, Amazon Kindle Direct, or Indie Author Project / Biblioboard.
     3	
     4	
     5	 Many authors have strong opinions about which publishing path is best. Traditional publishing
     6	offers support from a full team of experts, including editors, designers, and salespeople, often
     7	leading to higher sales and a more polished product. However, traditional publishing is notoriously
     8	slow and has historically excluded writers from marginalized groups. Self-publishing offers a
     9	quicker way to share your book with readers, as well as freedom from industry pressure to write
    10	something “sellable.”
    11	
    12	
    13	 However, self-published books can suffer from the lack of professional editing and design, and
    14	self-published authors take on the hard work of sales, marketing, and distribution.
    15	
    16	
    17	 There’s no one right answer. It depends on your personal goals for writing and publication. Below
    18	are three questions to help you decide whether traditional publishing or self-publishing is right
    19	for you.
    20	
    21	
    22	 You want to spend it writing, of course! However, writing is only one part of an author’s career.
    23	Authors also spend time revising, marketing their books, and, if you’re pursuing traditional
    24	publishing, finding an agent.
    25	
    26	
    27	 Most major publishers do not accept submissions directly from writers. Instead, writers find agents
    28	who sell their work to publishers in return for around 15% of profits. Having an agent signals to
    29	publishers that your book is good enough for at least one person to stake their career on it. And
    30	having an agent means you can focus on writing your next book instead of researching every editor at
    31	every imprint of every publishing house, and then becoming an expert in negotiating your own
    32	publishing contract.
    33	
    34	
    35	 However, you will have to put that research and negotiation power toward querying agents. During
    36	the querying process, writers email a brief pitch of their work to agents who may be interested.
    37	Querying is often considered one of the most difficult parts of traditional publishing, as writers
    38	may receive hundreds of rejections over multiple books.
    39	
    40	
    41	 Rejection isn’t always bad, though. It can be an invitation to revise and improve your work.
    42	Writing is hard, and no one gets it right on the first try. Early drafts of a book get the idea out
    43	of your brain and into words. Later drafts make the story reach its full potential.
    44	
    45	
    46	 Traditional publishing has multiple rounds of agent and editor revisions baked into the process.
    47	Self-publishing does not. Self-published writers decide for themselves how much to revise their work
    48	before sharing it. Some self-published authors hire freelance editors. Some trust friends and family
    49	for feedback. Others skip revisions, share the work as-is, and move on to their next project.
    50	Skipping revisions can have negative impacts on book quality, but ultimately, it’s a question of
    51	whether you’d prefer to spend your time telling new stories or polishing old ones.
    52	
    53	
    54	 Before publication, it may seem like traditional publishing takes a lot more work than
    55	self-publishing. However, once a book is published, the tables turn.
    56	
    57	
    58	 Traditional publishing includes whole teams of people working behind the scenes to determine how
    59	much books should cost, negotiate deals with booksellers, review books so teachers and librarians
    60	know which ones to buy, and more. If you’re self-publishing, you are those teams of people. You do
    61	all the work of pricing, formatting, selling, marketing, distributing, and more. Even if you only
    62	want to e-publish, you still have to format your own manuscript, or hire a professional to do it for
    63	you, and submit to the online platform(s) of your choice. You have to figure out a marketing
    64	strategy that will make you stand out, not only among self-published or indie authors, but also
    65	against professional marketing teams from billion-dollar publishing companies. It’s hard work! And
    66	it takes time away from writing.
    67	
    68	
    69	 Whether you choose traditional or self-publishing, writing is only one aspect of your career. It’s
    70	worth asking whether you’d prefer to spend time querying agents or becoming an expert in everything
    71	from typesetting to book distribution. It’s also worth considering why you want a writing career in
    72	the first place.
    73	
    74	
    75	 Every writer has their own reasons for writing. We love it. We don’t know how to live without it.
    76	We want to tell our story or make the world a better place.
    77	
    78	
    79	 Usually, the answer is not money.
    80	
    81	
    82	 And that’s okay! Creative expression can be fun and freeing and deeply meaningful, even if you
    83	never monetize it. If you know up front—before sending 100 query letters or spending hours and hours
    84	typesetting your manuscript—that writing is not a financial or career goal, you can save yourself a
    85	lot of stress and rejection.
    86	
    87	
    88	 However, if you do want to make writing a financially viable career, it’s important to know how and
    89	when you get paid through traditional or self-publishing.
    90	
    91	
    92	 In traditional publishing, when your agent sells your book to a publisher, you are paid an advance.
    93	An advance is a lump sum that the company expects to earn back later through your book sales.
    94	Advances vary wildly in amount. Small, indie publishers might pay as low as $1,000-$2,000. Large
    95	publishers might offer up to six figures or more. The amount depends on factors like genre, target
    96	age group, and whether it’s your first book or you’re more advanced in your career. After your book
    97	earns out its advance—meaning the publisher made back the money they paid you—then you earn
    98	royalties on every additional copy sold.
    99	
   100	
   101	 In traditional publishing, writers do not pay anything up front. If your agent or editor charges
   102	“reading fees,” or if you are asked to pay for any part of book design or production, you are being
   103	scammed. This is an important distinction because self-publishing works differently.
   104	
   105	
   106	 In self-publishing, your income depends entirely on how many books you sell. There are no advances.
   107	You may also have to pay up-front, depending on which parts of book production you want to tackle
   108	yourself and which parts (if any) you’d like to hire experts to manage for you. Up-front
   109	self-publishing costs could include hiring a freelance editor or book designer, or paying to print
   110	your book if you plan to sell hard copies. There are free e-publishing options, such as Kindle
   111	Direct or Indie Author Project / Biblioboard. For hard copies, a print-on-demand model like
   112	IngramSpark can save you from paying to print and warehouse extra books that you’re unable to sell.
   113	
   114	
   115	 It can be difficult to know whether it’s financially better to shop around your manuscript a little
   116	longer, waiting for that big advance, or whether you should go ahead and self-publish to start
   117	selling copies now. The answer can depend on what genre you’re writing in and what age group you’re
   118	writing for.
   119	
   120	
   121	 Your book’s length and genre, as well as the age of your readers, can have a huge impact on whether
   122	you’re able to make money in traditional or self-publishing. Sometimes, both can be profitable.
   123	
   124

   131	companies or self-published to readers, unless you’re already famous. Niche topics, like regional
   132	history, might have too small an audience for big publishers to profit, making self-publishing the

Based on `doc.txt`, here is what the document says:

**Differences between the two routes**

- *Traditional publishing* offers support from a full team of experts (editors, designers, salespeople), often leading to higher sales and a more polished product. However, it is notoriously slow and has historically excluded writers from marginalized groups. Most major publishers do not accept submissions directly from writers; instead, writers find agents who sell their work to publishers in return for around 15% of profits. Querying agents is often considered one of the most difficult parts, as writers may receive hundreds of rejections over multiple books. Traditional publishing also has multiple rounds of agent and editor revisions baked into the process.
- *Self-publishing* (through platforms like IngramSpark, Amazon Kindle Direct, or Indie Author Project / Biblioboard) offers a quicker way to share your book with readers and freedom from industry pressure to write something "sellable." However, self-published books can suffer from the lack of professional editing and design, and self-published authors take on the hard work of sales, marketing, and distribution. Self-published writers decide for themselves how much to revise (hiring freelance editors, trusting friends and family, or skipping revisions).
- *Workload timing:* Before publication, traditional publishing may seem to take more work, but once a book is published, the tables turn. In traditional publishing, teams handle pricing, negotiating with booksellers, and reviews; if you self-publish, you are those teams, doing all the pricing, formatting, selling, marketing, and distributing — even for e-publishing, which still requires formatting and submitting to platforms.
- *Payment:* In traditional publishing, you are paid an advance (a lump sum the company expects to earn back through sales), ranging from as low as $1,000–$2,000 at small indie publishers to six figures or more at large publishers, depending on genre, target age group, and career stage. After the advance is earned out, you earn royalties on every additional copy. Writers pay nothing up front; if an agent or editor charges "reading fees" or asks you to pay for design or production, you are being scammed. In self-publishing, income depends entirely on how many books you sell, there are no advances, and you may have to pay up front (e.g., for a freelance editor, designer, or printing). Free e-publishing options exist, and print-on-demand models like IngramSpark can save you from paying to print and warehouse unsold copies.

**How to know which route to take**

The document says there's no one right answer — it depends on your personal goals for writing and publication. It suggests considering:
- Whether you'd prefer to spend your time querying agents or becoming an expert in everything from typesetting to book distribution.
- Why you want a writing career in the first place. Usually, the answer is not money, and that's okay; if you know up front that writing is not a financial or career goal, you can save yourself a lot of stress and rejection.
- If you do want to make writing a financially viable career, it's important to know how and when you get paid through each route.

**Which route has the potential for greater profit**

The document does not declare one route more profitable. It says it can be difficult to know whether it's financially better to shop around your manuscript longer, waiting for a big advance, or to self-publish to start selling copies now, and that the answer can depend on what genre you're writing in and what age group you're writing for. A book's length and genre, and the age of your readers, can have a huge impact on whether you can make money in traditional or self-publishing, and sometimes both can be profitable. Specific examples given:
- *Romance* is a rare genre that both tops traditional publishing sales and has recently seen significant income growth for self-published authors; many romance writers are now "hybrid," writing both ways.
- *Memoirs* are notoriously hard to sell either way unless you're already famous.
- *Niche topics* (like regional history) may have too small an audience for big publishers to profit, making self-publishing the only way to share the information.
- *Children's books* tend to struggle with self-publishing, since many self-published books are e-books only, fewer children have e-readers, and most children's books are bought by adults looking for physical gifts.
